screening_decisions.reason: Randomised double-blind trial of intravenous aminophylline (theophylline analogue) vs placebo in 46 patients with acute ischaemic stroke. Treatment started within days of stroke onset and clinical outcomes were measured.

Randomised double-blind trial comparing intravenous aminophylline with placebo in 79 patients with acute cerebral infarction. Immediate neurological improvement was assessed, and treatment was initiated during the acute phase (within one week of onset).
Open-label, single-arm dose-escalation study without randomisation or a concurrent control group. Does not meet the minimum design requirement of a randomised controlled trial.

Studies the drug vincamin, not a theophylline analogue. No mention of participants having acute ischaemic stroke. Aminophylline was given to only 12 subjects, but the main intervention is vincamin and the population is not a stroke cohort.

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of oral caffeine in 19 patients recovering from acute ischaemic stroke. Caffeine is a methylxanthine analogue of theophylline. The exact timing of treatment onset is not stated, but patients are in the subacute recovery phase; conservative inclusion is warranted.

Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 250 mg caffeine in 20 patients recovering from acute ischaemic stroke. Caffeine is a relevant analogue. Despite no explicit statement about time from stroke onset, the acute stroke context suggests early treatment; included conservatively.

Study assesses cerebral blood flow after aminophylline infusion in 12 patients, but there is no indication that these patients had confirmed or presumed acute ischaemic stroke. Population does not meet the review criteria.
Animal study (cats with middle cerebral artery occlusion), not a human trial. Does not meet the inclusion criterion of human participants with acute stroke.
Animal study in anesthetised dogs, not a randomised trial in human stroke patients. The population and intervention do not match the review criteria.
This is a historical review/commentary (cites studies from 1953–1964), not a randomised controlled trial. No primary data from a prospective randomised comparison are presented.
